svg.title: How an asset uuid becomes a handle to a decoded asset
svg.desc: A uuid is looked up in the asset index, whose entry gives the asset's type and where its bytes are: a loose file, a span of the pack, or a part of another asset. The I/O backend reads the raw bytes, from the disk or the pack. The reader checks them: a pack entry against the signed manifest's hash, any file against its type's size cap and its decoder's recognition of its first bytes. The decoder registered for the type turns the bytes into a typed asset within its limits, a panic caught. The service caches the asset and hands back a handle. A load does all of it on the calling thread; a request files it to the loading family, which decodes off the frame, and the asset lands at a frame boundary.
svg.text: load: every station on the calling thread, at once
request: filed → the loading family decodes off the frame → lands at a boundary

g.text: A uuid, looked up
The index maps each uuid to its metadata: its type ("texture", "mesh"…) and where
its bytes are — a loose file, a span of the pack, or a part of another asset, such as
a mesh inside a glTF. One hash-map lookup; no file is opened yet.
The bytes, read
The I/O backend reads the raw bytes: a FileLoader from the project's assets folder,
a PackLoader from data.pack, decompressing an LZ4 entry. A part of another asset has
no bytes of its own: its container's are read.
Everything above this station is the same in development and in a shipped game.
The bytes, checked
A pack entry must hash to what the signed manifest says. Any file must fit its type's
size cap at the project's trust, and its first bytes must be what its decoder reads.
A file refused here is never decoded, and is quarantined.
The guard and the quarantine are explained in Trust.
Decoded
The decoder registered under the type's name turns the bytes into a typed asset —
a CpuTexture, a Mesh, a SoundData — within its limits at that trust. A decoder that
panics is caught: the file is refused, the engine goes on.
Cached, handed back
The service keeps the asset under its uuid and hands back an AssetHandle: a shared
pointer, cheap to clone. Every later load of the uuid gets the same copy; many
entities showing one mesh share one copy in memory.
Two ways in
load walks the stations on the calling thread and returns the handle or the error.
request returns a cached copy at once, or files the decode: the loading family walks
the stations off the frame, and the copy lands in the service at a frame boundary.
The resolvers and the reload only request: no frame waits for the disk.
